Flagrant

FLAY-grunt -- Latin flagrare, 'to burn, blaze': a flagrant offense burns in plain sight. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Flagrant is openly and offensively wrong, with no attempt to hide it.

Copying an entire essay word for word is a flagrant case of cheating.

Worked Example

A driver rolls slowly past a stopped school bus with its red lights flashing and its stop arm out, waves at the bus driver, and keeps going.

Wrongdoing done openly, with no attempt to hide it, is exactly what flagrant describes. Unlike 'serious,' which is only about size, flagrant is about how plainly wrong the act is and how little the offender cares who sees.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

blatant: Blatant means done openly, with no attempt to hide it. Flagrant goes further: a flagrant act is not only open but plainly and offensively wrong. A loud yawn in class is blatant rudeness; shoving a referee is flagrant misconduct.

shameless: Shameless describes the offender's attitude -- feeling no embarrassment at all about what they have done. Flagrant describes the act itself: wrongdoing so open and so plainly wrong that everyone can see it. A shameless person may still operate in secret; a flagrant act never hides.

glaring: Glaring means so obvious it almost hurts to look at, and it usually attaches to errors and flaws -- a glaring typo, a glaring omission. Flagrant adds shamelessness and real wrongdoing: a mistake can be glaring, but only misconduct is flagrant.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

concealed: kept out of sight

trivial: too small to matter

Where it sits · how plainly wrong the act is — obvious → flagrant → outrageous

obvious vs. flagrant: Obvious is neutral where flagrant is damning. An obvious answer is simply easy to see, while a flagrant act is committed openly and is plainly wrong.

outrageous vs. flagrant: Outrageous is flagrant plus fury: a flagrant violation is openly and offensively wrong. An outrageous one is wrong enough to make people genuinely angry.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — flagr-

root — flagr-: to burn, to blaze (Latin (flagrare))

suffix — -ant

suffix — -ant: adjective-forming: doing the action (Latin (-antem))

Put it together

Put it together: Latin flagrans meant 'blazing, burning,' from flagrare ('to burn') -- a flagrant offense blazes away in full view of everyone, from the same root behind conflagration, a great fire.

Use the root in a new word: conflagration

Use the root in a new word: conflagration: A single spilled lantern grew into a conflagration that swept through six blocks.

Word Choice

Flagrant attaches to wrongdoing: a flagrant foul, a flagrant lie, a flagrant violation. It always disapproves, and it stresses that the offender did not even bother to hide what they were doing.
